article.overview: A biological tissue exposure experiment places living biological material, such as cells, tissue models or small organisms, inside a controlled container or instrument, exposes it to space or lunar-surface conditions and records the effects. The conditions of interest on the Moon are mainly ionising radiation, the near absence of an atmosphere, large temperature swings and, in cislunar flight, reduced gravity. The catalogue name describes a class of experiments rather than one standard instrument. The examples reviewed here show that the category is currently dominated by plants, yeast and radiation-dosimetry instruments on the lunar surface and in lunar orbit, with one crew-flown human-tissue experiment in cislunar space.
article.description: In this category, a tissue exposure experiment usually combines four elements: a biological sample (for example bone-marrow-derived cells in a microfluidic organ chip, or a yeast, seed or silkworm culture in a sealed container); a containment and life-support arrangement that keeps the sample alive; a radiation or environmental measurement; and a control or return path for comparison on the ground. Lunar-surface designs also depend on a lander or relay for power, thermal management and data. This article uses the catalogue name as a broad description and reports only what the consulted sources support. Where a source describes a different organism or hardware item from the one implied by the catalogue name, the difference is stated rather than resolved [1][2].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: Such experiments aim to show how lunar or deep-space conditions affect living systems, so that crews and future biological payloads can be designed to protect them. NASA states that AVATAR investigates how deep-space radiation and microgravity affect human health, with the goal of protecting astronauts as exploration expands [2]. The LEIA mission page states that its aim is to deliver yeast to the lunar surface to help prepare humans for travel to the Moon and Mars, using yeast because its DNA-damage repair processes resemble those of humans [1]. The CRaTER instrument is a dosimetry sensor rather than a biology experiment, but its stated purpose is to investigate the effects of shielding by measuring the energy-transfer spectrum behind tissue-equivalent plastic [4]. Applications named by NASA include astronaut health and safety and microbial food and drug production on the Moon and Mars [1].
article.operating_principle: In the reviewed examples the biological sample is held in a controlled environment and its response is compared with a ground reference. AVATAR's organ chips are operated by a pressure-driven microfluidic system that supplies nutrients and removes waste, with the environment held at 37 degrees Celsius; the payload runs autonomously after activation on the ground [3]. Its samples are to be analysed after return and compared with a simultaneous ground control study, with single-cell RNA sequencing planned to measure gene-expression changes [3]. Dosimetry instruments such as CRaTER work differently: particles deposit energy in a tissue-equivalent material, and detectors record how that energy is distributed, which helps constrain models of biological radiation effects [4]. Descriptions of the Chang'e-4 payload report a sealed container in which organisms would exchange gases, a design intended to sustain a small closed ecosystem [6].
article.scientific_importance: Living tissue responds to radiation through DNA damage, repair and cell-cycle effects, which differ from the responses of electronics or structural materials. Flown tissue experiments can therefore test assumptions that ground radiation facilities cannot fully reproduce, such as combined radiation and microgravity exposure [2][3]. However, no AVATAR results were published in the sources reviewed, and sample analysis had not been reported at the time of this review. For the lunar surface, the scientific return of the category is therefore currently based on planned or early experiments rather than on a body of published results.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a biological tissue exposure experiment. The four examples below differ in purpose, host platform and hardware, so their dimensions, masses and power values are not directly comparable. Values are given only where a consulted source states them; otherwise they are recorded as not publicly specified in this run.

examples.name: Chang'e-4 Biological Experiment Payload (formerly reported as Lunar Micro Ecosystem)
examples.type: Reported flown lunar-surface biology payload (not a tissue experiment)
examples.status: Reported as part of the Chang'e-4 mission; outcome disputed across sources.
examples.organisms_per_secondary_reports: Secondary reports list different contents, including cotton seeds and yeast; manifest unresolved.
examples.container: Pre-launch coverage describes a sealed aluminium container for gas exchange among the organisms.
examples.outcome: Secondary reports state that cotton was the only organism to show results and that a cotton sprout died when temperatures fell after the first lunar day. Not checked against a CNSA or Chongqing University primary publication.

examples.name: Cosmic Ray Telescope for the Effects of Radiation (CRaTER) on the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter
examples.type: Flown lunar-orbit radiation dosimetry instrument (not a biology experiment)
examples.design_goal: Described as simple, compact, and comparatively low-cost, but with sufficiently large geometric factor for measuring linear energy transfer (LET) spectra.
examples.tissue_equivalent_plastic: The instrument measures radiation behind tissue-equivalent plastic, whose stated purpose is to investigate the effects of shielding. Detector type and plastic dimensions were not described on the consulted page.
examples.mission_context: LRO's primary mission is described as orbiting the Moon at about 50 km for one year, with a possible three-year science extension.

examples.name: A Virtual Astronaut Tissue Analog Response (AVATAR) on Artemis II
examples.type: Crew-flown experiment in cislunar space (not a lunar-surface payload)
examples.status: Reported flown on the Artemis II mission inside Orion during an approximately 10-day journey around the Moon. Results not published in sources reviewed.
examples.samples: Organ chips containing bone marrow tissue derived from cells of the Artemis II astronauts. NASA describes the chips as containing astronaut cells and modelling regions of organs such as brain, lungs, heart, pancreas and liver; the flown model is not specified.
examples.chip_size: Roughly the size of a USB thumb drive.
examples.hardware: Space Tango built the automated hardware, mounted on the Orion port wall of the environmental control and life support system (ECLSS). Pressure-driven microfluidics supplied nutrients and removed waste; environment held at 37 degrees Celsius. Payload ran autonomously; crew pressed a button once daily to confirm system health.
examples.power: Internal lithium-ion batteries designed to support 14 days of operation, with extra capacity covering three launch attempts.
examples.analysis_plan: Samples to be analysed after return and compared with a simultaneous ground control study; single-cell RNA sequencing planned.

examples.name: LEIA (Lunar Explorer Instrument for space biology Applications)
examples.type: Proposed lunar-surface biology payload (not flown according to consulted sources)
examples.organism: Yeast, used to study responses to radiation and reduced gravity, and to test antioxidant production.
examples.schedule: NASA mission page lists 2027 as the target year, without a month or day. Earlier coverage referred to a launch no earlier than 2026.
examples.components: NASA mission page describes yeast as the payload. Search-result summaries of a conference abstract describe a BioSensor, a charged particle detector and a mini fast neutron detector; these conflict with the NASA page and are unverified.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No universal dimensions exist for this payload class. The consulted sources give a USB-thumb-drive scale for AVATAR organ chips and no verified dimensions for the Chang'e-4 container, the CRaTER sensor or LEIA.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass is not publicly specified for any of the four examples in the consulted sources. Mission-level hardware mass for Orion, LRO or the lander is not the same as the mass of the biological exposure hardware and is not used here.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: AVATAR's batteries were designed for 14 days of operation. Power for the lunar-surface examples depends on the host lander or relay, which was not verified for any of them.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: The lunar surface combines a near-vacuum, large day-night temperature variation and high-energy radiation, and biological material also needs stable temperature, nutrient delivery and waste removal. AVATAR's flight hardware held its cells at 37 degrees Celsius and used an autonomous, battery-powered design. Surface experiments must therefore carry thermal control and power through the lunar night. This is a general engineering requirement for any surface biology payload, not a value verified for a particular example. Radiation exposure on the surface is a central motivation for LEIA, while CRaTER's shielding measurements show how radiation interacts with tissue-equivalent material. Dust, vibration and mechanical loads during landing and deployment are general considerations that were not quantified in the consulted sources.
article.limitations: A tissue exposure payload is limited by the lifetime of its life-support and power systems. AVATAR's batteries are designed for 14 days, which bounds the duration of the flown experiment. Surface payloads are additionally constrained by the thermal survival of their hardware, communication windows and the dependence on a lander for power and data. Biological payloads also face limits on sample count and on the ability to return samples for analysis.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Biological tissue exposure payloads in this set use three different delivery contexts, and the transportation considerations differ between them. The Chang'e-4 and LEIA examples are lunar-surface payloads, CRaTER is an orbiter instrument, and AVATAR is a crew-flown experiment integrated into Orion. The paragraphs below are general engineering descriptions. They do not assert compatibility with any named lander or spacecraft beyond the host documented in the sources.
transportation_process: Integrate the surface payload into a lander or deployable package on Earth.
Launch the payload and transfer it to the Moon.
Land the payload and supply power, thermal control and a data link.
For CRaTER, operate the instrument within the orbiter's orbit, power and data systems.
For AVATAR, mount the hardware inside Orion, activate it on the ground before launch, and return the samples with the crew for analysis after splashdown.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Surface examples require a lander or deployable package; no deployment mechanism was verified for LEIA or Chang'e-4. CRaTER requires no separate deployment because it is carried by LRO. AVATAR is mounted on Orion's port ECLSS wall and runs autonomously with a once-daily crew check.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Chang'e-4 (reported lunar-surface biology payload), CRaTER on LRO (flown lunar-orbit dosimetry instrument) and AVATAR on Artemis II (crew-flown cislunar experiment).
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No lander-specific compatibility is verified for LEIA, Chang'e-4 or CRaTER beyond the host documented in the sources. AVATAR's compatibility is with Orion as described by R&D World. The LEIA mission page names no lander or delivery vehicle.

article.historical_significance: Lunar biology and radiation-biology experiments are at an early stage. The Chang'e-4 payload is reported as one of the few attempts to grow living organisms on the lunar surface, but its results are disputed across sources. CRaTER forms part of LRO's radiation record, and its tissue-equivalent design links lunar measurements to biological dose concepts. AVATAR's flight is recent, and press coverage describes it as the first use of organ chips beyond low-Earth orbit; this claim was not verified against a NASA primary text in this run. BioSentinel, a yeast-based biology CubeSat that flew on Artemis I, is cited in search results as a precursor to LEIA; its fact sheet was not parsed in this run.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: No single standard design exists for this payload class, so the examples are not interchangeable. Only one example (AVATAR) involves human-derived tissue, and it flew in cislunar space rather than on the lunar surface. No AVATAR results were published in the consulted sources, and the Chang'e-4 manifest and outcome conflict between sources. The examples are therefore best read as individual case records rather than as a comparable set.

data_quality_notes: Catalogue name 'Biological tissue exposure experiment' is a broad class name; no single standard design was identified. Examples are chosen to illustrate the class and are not interchangeable.

Only AVATAR involves human-derived tissue, and it flew on Artemis II in cislunar space, not on the lunar surface. No AVATAR results were published in the consulted sources; sample analysis is planned after return.

Chang'e-4 payload manifest conflicts between the Chongqing University image caption (silkworms, potato seeds, Arabidopsis seeds) and secondary reports (cotton, yeast, fruit fly eggs, rape seeds). Outcome from secondary reports only; not checked against CNSA or Chongqing University primary publications.

LEIA: NASA mission page (last updated 17 December 2025) lists yeast as the only payload and 2027 as the target year. Search-result summaries of a conference abstract describe additional detectors (BioSensor, charged particle detector, mini fast neutron detector) and a south polar CLPS delivery; these were not verified against NASA primary text and conflict with the NASA page.

CRaTER mass, dimensions and power were not publicly specified in the consulted sources. The CRaTER instrument description (2010) and shielding results reported in 2013 coverage were not checked against primary papers in this run.

Image verification: LEIA mission-page JPEG confirmed to resolve as a direct asset; its visual content was not reviewed. Chang'e-4 and AVATAR images have no verified direct asset URL and are referenced by source page only.
BioSentinel fact sheet (NASA PDF) could not be parsed in this run; its reference is retained for context only and is not used for any specification.
